name: Bias in Clinical Triage
title: Bias in Clinical Triage
answer: Bias in clinical triage refers to systematic differences in how an AI system assigns urgency, acuity, or priority to patients based on characteristics such as race, sex, age, language, insurance status, or disability. The concern spans pre-hospital dispatch, emergency department waiting rooms, inpatient early warning scores, and telehealth symptom checkers. It includes bias introduced by training data, outcome labels, feature choices, and the way clinicians override or accept model recommendations. This page treats bias as a governance and safety problem, not only a statistical one.

sections.body: Bias in clinical triage refers to systematic differences in how an AI system assigns urgency, acuity, or priority to patients based on characteristics such as race, sex, age, language, insurance status, or disability. The concern spans pre-hospital dispatch, emergency department waiting rooms, inpatient early warning scores, and telehealth symptom checkers. It includes bias introduced by training data, outcome labels, feature choices, and the way clinicians override or accept model recommendations. This page treats bias as a governance and safety problem, not only a statistical one.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Triage models typically run inside hospital electronic health record workflows, on ambulance tablets, in patient-facing symptom checkers, and in call center decision support tools. They draw on structured fields such as vital signs, lab results, and chief complaints, as well as free-text nursing notes and demographic data. Some are cloud-hosted and updated centrally, while others are embedded in medical devices or run on local servers to meet latency and privacy requirements. The same model may be deployed across multiple sites with different patient populations, which can amplify bias if not monitored.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams audit triage models by comparing error rates across patient groups, especially false negatives for high-acuity conditions such as sepsis, stroke, or myocardial infarction. They examine calibration, meaning whether predicted risk matches observed outcomes within each group, and they test for disparate impact in who gets assigned a lower priority. Common corrections include reweighting training data, removing or adjusting proxy variables, and setting group-specific decision thresholds. Human review of near-miss cases and shadow deployments are used to catch bias that only appears in live use.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Bias in triage sits under medical device regulation, data protection law, and hospital quality and safety obligations. The atlas records six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows how biased triage decisions can become legal and evidentiary records. Provenance matters: a model's training data, validation population, and update history should be documented so that bias can be traced to its source. Risk management includes bias monitoring plans, incident reporting, and clear rules for when clinicians may override a triage score.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Triage AI is moving toward prospective validation in diverse health systems, continuous monitoring of subgroup performance, and standardized fairness metrics that regulators and purchasers can compare. Federated learning and privacy-preserving audits may allow bias checks across institutions without pooling sensitive patient data. Expect more emphasis on explainable triage scores, human oversight requirements, and post-market surveillance as part of device clearance. The field is shifting from one-time bias audits to ongoing governance that treats fairness as a maintenance task.
